newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian 97/98 coffee/cocoa farmgate prices seen up.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian 97/98 coffee/cocoa farmgate prices seen up.

text.p: Ivory Coast is likely to raise its reference cocoa and coffee farmgate prices in the 1997/98 (Oct-Sept) season, upcountry buyers and exporters say.
"My feeling is that we will have a rise for both cocoa and coffee," said one industry buyer. "There are a number of elements pointing to an increase, but none to a decrease."
Donors in 1996/97 have pushed for increases as part of talks on disbursement of outstanding amounts of a $150 million agricultural sector adjustment loan from the World Bank.
"They will probably give 10 percent more of the export price to farmers but we are still waiting for a response," said one donor after recent talks failed to end in agreement.

Ivory Coast has put off donor-sponsored market liberalisation plans until 1998/99 for coffee, and 1999/2000 for cocoa. Details have yet to be finalised but include plans for scrapping official marketing price lists, or "baremes".

"For now the baremes are alive, even if in a looser form," said one exporter, who also expected rises. "It would certainly keep donors happy as Ivorian farmers are still not paid much compared to others (in the world)."
Ivory Coast set a cocoa farmgate price of 315 CFA a kilo for 1996/97, unchanged from the f1995/96 year, although export duties were cut.

Coffee prices were set 200 CFA lower at 495 CFA. Industry analysts say the state Caistab marketing body, which used to have a monopoly on marketing, made losses on payments to exporters as world prices fell in 1995/96.

Industry sources say Caistab funds for cocoa and coffee are both in surplus. Buoyant world prices since late 1996 had resulted in large reverse payments by exporters earning over and above bareme-designated export rates, they said.

Agricultural experts say Ivorian cocoa farmers receive one of the lowest percentages of export values in the world -- about 44 percent of Free-On-Board prices compared to up to 85 percent at times in countries such as Indonesia.

"The margin of state profits from cocoa have been in a comfortable position for some time," said one industry buyer pointing to a flat cocoa farmgate price for the past three years. "I would not rule out 100 CFA (a kilo) rises."

Neighbouring quality cocoa producer Ghana said after raising its official farmgate price for late 1996/97 crop by 50 percent to 1.8 million cedis per tonne that farmers were getting 54 percent of FOB prices. Ghana aims to raise that to 60 percent by 2000.
Ivorian buyers say they applied discounts in 1996/97 as quality problems arose in cocoa and particularly coffee sectors. Some coffee buyers paid above reference rates for top grades.
Some analysts say quality problems stem from past reforms, including closure of upcountry state buying centres in 1995.
Leeway for price-setting margins for buyers is unclear under Ivorian law, buyers say. Industry buyers want the Caistab to step out of price-setting altogether and act as an industry support agency.
Crop analysts say a cocoa price rise from 315 would make sense in the context of donor pressure for a rise.
"It would prepare for a rise before introduction of the overall policy (in 2000)," said one. "I would not rule out 400 CFA." Another said trade talk centred around 375 CFA.
"With coffee you have to be more careful," said one analyst. "World prices were fluctuating about like crazy all year but, that said, a rise of 100 CFA would still be safe."
